title: Can a robot nail wall sheathing to code tolerance, and what decides it?
lede: research programme on robotic sheathing of a wood-frame wall; milestone 1: APA's 1/8 in gap shrinks the joint-nail window to ±3.14 mm and sheets must hang plumb to about 0.03°; milestone 2: a bowed stud moves under the straight sheet edge, so at published stud warp a robot reading each stud once gets 55% clean sheets, three reads 80% and perfect sensing 87%, while a 3x or doubled 2x at the joints (as the shear-wall standard allows) gives 100% with three reads; milestone 4: tacking the sheet and aiming from its measured edge lets a robot hang it to 0.54° and 10 mm (1σ) on doubled joints, 18 times coarser than the 0.03° single-2x joints need, where re-hanging tops out at 87% clean; milestone 3 (first part, MuJoCo): a sheet lowered onto a ledger and released seats to 0.0001° if the robot presses under about 100 N, and then PS 2 panel squareness leaves 100% clean sheets on doubled joints but at most 84–95% on single 2x; milestone 3 (second part): a stock Unitree G1 holds at most 8.7 kg and an H1 18.8 kg, so neither can carry the 21.8 kg sheet, but on the ledger both press it (66–110 N, 128–281 N) and at Unitree's own joint gains both are soft enough for the ledger to seat it, except an H1 with a rigid clamp; push below W/(2μ) when sliding it or it tips; milestone 5: with every stage of the cycle charged (place, sense, nail, re-drive missed nails), two 2x at the joint and one read a stud give 99.94% clean sheets in 76–216 s, while the best single-2x pipeline gets 56% and is 18–65 s slower a sheet, which is what the extra joint stud may cost to frame; milestone 7: priced in dollars, a G1 on a drive-and-lift base is the cheapest robot (it beats a walking H1 in every draw) and beats a hand crew's $5.21 a sheet in 37% of draws at 100 houses a year and 74% at 300, a gantry wins only from about 500 houses a year, and the extra joint stud ($5.42 a sheet) never pays unless a missed nail costs about $6.50 more than its re-drive; milestone 6: on a second physics engine (Drake) every ledger pipeline's clean-sheet rate holds within 0.05 points; milestone 6b: a smoothly bowed sheet edge is a stable rocker (radius 117 m), so the 0.149° bow rock was a three-foot modelling artefact and the best single-2x pipeline rises from 56% to 62.5% clean sheets, while a kink or 1 mm of grit on the ledger keeps a rock of up to 0.09–0.15°; milestone 8: the paper draft for Automation in Construction, every quoted number checked against its results file; milestone 9: pushing a bowed joint stud onto its line takes 28–126 N (99th percentile, published warp), within a stock G1's 81–88 N sideways push, and lifts single-2x joints from 56% to 71% clean sheets at low warp and 31% to 68% at high, but not to 95%, because straight studs cap the same pipeline at 74%; milestone 10: that ceiling is shared by the nail gun's 0.9 mm scatter (45–47% of the misses) and the sheet's pose (39–44%), which only fail together; sliding the sheet to centre its gap and shimming it plumb lift single 2x to 92–94%, and 95% then needs a tool held to about 0.8 mm; milestone 11: the first measured studs, six from a public laser scan of a robot-built 2x4 wall, bow by the published amount (median 0.106 in at 8 ft) but are not parabolas, and on their real shapes single 2x falls to 43–47% clean sheets against 58% for parabolas, while doubled joints stay at 100%; milestone 12: reading each measured stud at every nail height recovers most of that loss (43% to 53%), a mid push still adds 13 points, and with a slide and shim single 2x reaches 77%, short of the 92% straight studs allow; doubled joints stay at 100%; milestone 13: priced per clean sheet on those measured studs, the remedies are cheap (the full single-2x stack costs $7.42 a sheet against $7.10 for three reads alone at 100 houses a year, for 77% first-pass clean sheets against 43%), the doubled joint stud still costs $5.13 a sheet more than the cheapest single-2x pipeline in every draw, and it pays only if a missed nail costs about $5.51 more than its re-drive; milestone 14: a missed nail nobody finds costs about 2% of its sheet's racking capacity in a rigid-plastic shear-wall model, but misses cluster (99th-percentile sheet loses 11.5% with three reads), and nailing single-2x joint edges at 4 in instead of 6 in carries every escaped miss for less than re-driving them; milestone 15: rebuilt as a framed-sheet limit analysis with stud-to-plate joints at NDS strength, the model still loses only 20% with the bottom foot unnailed, so weak end-nail joints do not explain tested walls' 50% loss (it needs joints at half the NDS ratio, or no hold-downs), while a lone sheet whose top plate can tilt loses 17% at the escaped-miss tail and 4 in joint edges carry the misses under every joint model; milestone 16: with each nail on a tested 8d-in-OSB backbone that peaks and softens, the sheet peaks at 9.8 kN (551 plf) and the unnailed bottom foot still costs only 20%, because a racking sheet slips its perimeter nails almost equally, so softening nails are ruled out too and the anchorage is what is left; milestone 17: built as Weiss (2017) tested it (two sheets, hold-downs only at the wall's ends) the model matches her controls' spacing ratio, but at code-strength stud-to-plate joints her decayed walls would keep 80% and 63%, not the 57% and 34% she measured; end nails at 0.47 of the NDS ratio fit both, because the decayed wall then slides on its sill nails whatever the sheathing schedule, and an escaped miss still costs about 2.7% of a wall; milestone 18: adding the hold-downs' anchor rods, which pass through the sill, stops that slide at about 420 lb a rod, below the rod's own NDS design value (617 lb), and then no end-nail strength fits the 3 in wall (it keeps 64–74% against 34% tested); a fit needs the rods and the end nails both below their design values, so slack, splitting or cyclic tear-out is what is left, and an escaped miss still costs 2–3% of a wall; milestone 19: the same wall as a displacement model with tested nail curves, softening stud joints and slack at the anchor rods reproduces the rigid-plastic limit to 0.04%, but slack (1/16 in moves the decayed walls 0.1 point) and early-peaking joints do not explain the 3 in wall: all 30 fits within 5 points need end nails at a quarter of their NDS ratio; milestone 20: under the CUREE cyclic protocol with pinching (SAWS) nails fitted to Weiss’s materials and checked against OpenSees, the decayed 3 in wall keeps 70.6% against 70.5% pushed once, so cyclic loading does not explain the 34%; fits still need end nails at a quarter of their NDS ratio; milestone 21: nails whose strength falls with the energy they dissipate (the Rahnama–Krawinkler rule, rate swept) cut the intact walls’ cyclic peaks by up to 37% but raise the decayed walls’ shares by 0.3–2.9 points at code-strength joints (70.6% to 73.5%), because intact walls work their sheathing nails harder; damage spread by energy cannot produce the 34%, and the best fit is still end nails at a quarter of NDS with no degradation; milestone 27: sliding the sheet along the ledger leaves 0.19–0.64 mm only if the robot drops its push within 20 ms of the sheet moving, and 2.5–10 mm at 100 ms, where the best single-2x stack falls from 0.77 to 0.32; milestone 28: a stack of 1/16 in shims plumbs the sheet to 0.46 mm rms (as good as assumed), while driving a tapered shim needs about 119 N, which a stock G1 cannot push low on the wall; milestone 29: the 0.9 mm tool scatter was the hand, not the nailer: carried to a nose 0.3 m ahead and 44 mm into the stud, a stock G1 leaves 1.3 mm and the best single-2x stack falls from 0.80 to 0.26, while 12-bit joint sensors restore 0.93; milestone 30: gear backlash costs only on joints nothing holds, the G1's two ankle rolls at the stud pose: 5 arcmin unheld takes the 12-bit stack from 0.93 to 0.77, biasing the ankle rolls one way removes the loss; milestone 31: across the poses along a wall three held joints flip sign, so one calibration leaves up to 3.4 mm and 12-bit joints tolerate 0.44 arcmin of backlash, against 2.5 calibrated pose by pose; milestone 32: pushing through real soles, a G1 standing upright balances only 26–39 N of press above 0.8 m, so it must lean into the wall, and on the leaned poses no ground-reaction split removes the need to compensate backlash pose by pose (one calibration still leaves 1.1–2.6 mm); milestone 33: compensating backlash pose by pose from predicted torques removes that residual only when the compensator models the robot's own balance controller (then a full nail magazine left out of the model costs 0.02 mm); a wrong ground-reaction model leaves 1.2–1.9 mm; milestone 34: under the press, joints must be stiffer than about 1.8×10⁴ N m/rad if the nose can slide on the sheet (1×10⁴ if friction holds it, which it does at 10 of 15 G1 poses), and an unmodelled nail magazine droops Unitree's PD servos by 32–51 mm; milestone 35: a dragged air hose is a force the compensator cannot know: 5 N leaves 1.0 mm and 0–10 N of drag costs 21 points; milestone 36: a wrist force-torque sensor cuts 0–20 N of hose drag from 91.6 points lost to 1.6, but any sensor error flips held joints at the friction threshold, leaving 0.3–0.8 mm; milestone 37: a 0.1 N m preload on the leg joints removes the flips the balance controller causes by holding joints exactly at the threshold (0–20 N back from 56.5 points lost to 1.6), but the 0.3–0.8 mm left is in the waist and arms; milestone 38: a two-hand squeeze along the grip line moves only the arm joints, clears every arm flip and takes 0–20 N of hose drag from 1.6 points lost to 0.05, leaving a 0.5 mm floor in the waist; milestone 39: a braked waist takes that floor to 0.01 mm (a 1 arcmin waist gearbox to 0.11), while locking roll and pitch as on the base G1 does nothing because the yaw is what flips; milestone 40: the nailer's recoil, bracketed at 0.09–8.7 N s from published measurements, lifts the nose, but the re-press sets none of the joints left loose (most change sign inside the press window), so the 0.012 mm spec stands, while 12 of 35 leaned stances cannot stand without the press; milestone 41: re-leaning 10–39 mm lets every one of those stances stand at zero press and still take 50 N with the 0.011 mm spec intact, but only below a grip height of 1.225 m on the G1 (1.6 N to spare at 1.2 m) and at a cost of 1.3 points of clean sheets; milestone 42: that 1.3 points is all the lean (the controller's four flipped leg-joint sides change no stack but keep one pose holdable), and like for like the H1 loses only 0.09–0.29 points per pose; milestone 43: in the spec's own plan the zero-press stance gains the G1 1 point at its worst pose (0.9160 to 0.9257), and the cost moves to the H1, which keeps a plan at only 3 of 6 re-leaned poses; milestone 44: a per-pose leg preload (0.030 and 0.085 N m) gives both poses a plan at no clean-sheet cost, but only (1.6 m, 0) meets the tool-point spec (0.003 mm); at (1.4 m, −0.15 m) the right hip roll flips and leaves 0.17 mm; milestone 45: a hold-first preload cannot fix it (the stance caps that joint at 0.0339 N m), so that pose needs a wrist sensor with under about 0.19 N of z error; milestone 46: that joint was held on the wrong side; held on the other side the pose takes the full preload and leaves 0.005 mm, so the H1 meets the tool-point spec at all 19 poses with an FT 300; milestone 47: per-pose hold sides lift every pose's margin, rescue two H1 poses and cut the H1's worst residual at 20 N drag to 0.010 mm, but push the G1 to 0.037 mm, so sides must be scored under drag; milestone 48: sides scored over the hose sweep return the G1 to 0.011 mm at 20 N and keep the H1's 0.010, but no side holds a 20 N backward drag at 8 of 34 poses and the G1's worst residuals cover 83% of the swept cases; milestone 51: every swept case past those drag limits has no plan, and inside them the G1 plans 93% (from 83%), but most of what is left is its one calibration pose under sideways drag, so calibrate with the hose slack; milestone 52: calibrating with the hose slack lifts the G1 to 98.1% with no residual change, since the calibration absorbs only the sensor bias; milestone 53: choosing the hold sides per measured hose load gives both robots a plan at 100% of cases inside the drag limits, in spec; milestone 55: a held-or-free margin sized from the sensor bound puts every planned case in spec (worst 0.011 mm, from 0.284) but drops 3 to 4% of cases, mostly at the waist, which nothing preloads; milestone 56: weighting that margin by each flip's cost at the nose keeps every planned case in spec (worst 0.018 mm) and restores coverage to 99.6 to 100%; milestone 58: pricing each flip across the wall too keeps every planned press inside 0.03 mm in both directions (worst 0.022 mm across, from 0.27–0.29) at the same coverage; milestone 59: the nail's depth point 44.4 mm in also stays inside 0.03 mm under that bound (tilt at most 0.034 mrad), so the angle needs no rows of its own
summary: A research programme (proposal and log on the project page) asking whether a stock humanoid, a mobile manipulator with a lift or a purpose-built gantry can hang a 4x8 sheet of wall sheathing and land all 62 nails where the panel maker and the code want them, which error source decides it, and what a clean sheet costs; it gathers track 20's 26 buildbot-* projects into one question aimed at Automation in Construction. Milestone 1 adds what earlier projects left out: panels are hung with a 1/8 in gap (APA's recommendation) centred on the joint stud, sheets are hung slightly off and out of plumb, and their width differs from the 48 in stud module. With the gap, the 34 joint nails' window shrinks from ±3.93 to ±3.14 mm, and the single stud reading needed for 95% clean sheets (0.9 mm tool scatter) falls from 0.90 to 0.41 mm; at buildbot-studfind's 0.89 mm only 75% of sheets come out clean, 56% if the robot does not plan for the gap. With a 0.5 mm stud reading, a robot aiming at the design window has no tolerance for sheet pose at all; aiming from the measured sheet edge (to 0.5 mm) allows 0.44 mm of translation and 0.031° of rotation (1σ), and halves the weight of the stud error. Along a 40 ft wall, sheets butted with a 1/8 in gauge drift 3.2 mm a sheet: no third sheet is clean with full panels, and panels trimmed 1/16 in keep a joint window for four sheets; setting each sheet from its own studs keeps every sheet at 98% clean. Milestone 2 lets the studs bow and twist as real lumber does. A Stud-grade 8 ft 2x4 may bow 3/4 in and twist 3/8 in, and published kiln-dried studs average 0.11–0.21 in of bow and 0.08–0.16 in of twist. Bow moves the 1.5 in nailing face under a sheet edge that stays straight, so a single-2x joint closes for any bow over 0.53 in, whatever the robot knows. At the lower published warp, one read per stud gives 55% clean sheets, three reads and a fitted curve 80%, perfect stud and edge sensing 87%; reaching 95% would mean rejecting about two thirds of studs for bow. Framing the joints with a 3x or two fastened 2x (named for adjoining panel edges in the shear-wall standard, SDPWS 4.3.7.1) widens the window by 1/2 in a side, and three reads then give 100% clean sheets at both warp levels; twist costs 1–2 points. Milestone 4 asks how coarsely a robot may hang the sheet if it tacks it with two field nails, measures where the edge landed and aims the joint nails from that, or re-hangs it when the window looks too tight. On single-2x joints the sheet must still hang to about 0.03° and 0.4 mm (1σ) for 95% clean sheets; re-hanging a 1 mm / 0.1° hang peaks at 87% (2.1 hangs a sheet), and a held sheet may sway only 0.19 mm under the nail. On two 2x fastened at the joint, tack-then-measure allows 0.54° and 10 mm at the lower published warp, and a held sheet may sway 4.1 mm: the placement target for the humanoid and lift experiments. Milestone 3, first part asks whether a ledger board under the sheet can do the squaring a robot cannot. In MuJoCo, a 21.8 kg sheet lowered 0.25–2° off plumb onto a level ledger and released ends within 0.0001° of it for any press up to 100 N; above 115–380 N (wall friction 0.7 to 0.2) friction holds the whole error, at 0.87–0.99 of the closed form, and a wrist that keeps over about 7,500 N·m/rad of stiffness at 1° keeps part of its own error. Seated, what is left is the panel (PS 2-18: 0.083° out of square, a 1/16 in edge bow that rocks it up to 0.149°) and a laser line rated 1/8 in at 30 ft: 100% clean sheets on doubled joints in every setting, 84–86% on single 2x with panels drawn up to the PS 2 limits, and 95% only if panels are within a quarter of them. Milestone 3, second part puts a stock Unitree G1 or H1 (MuJoCo Menagerie, static whole-body model, torque limits, no foot slip) in that holder's place. Neither can carry the sheet to the wall: the G1 holds at most 2.8–8.7 kg in both hands at 0.6–1.3 m and the H1 12.4–18.8 kg. With the sheet on the ledger, the G1 presses 66–110 N and the H1 128–281 N. Sliding the seated sheet to its stud line tips it unless pushed below W/(2μl) (MuJoCo within 1.6% in 14 cases); a G1 manages the slide at ledger friction 0.3 but not 0.5, and not through palm friction at all. At Unitree's published joint gains (G1 arms 60 N·m/rad) the sheet's stiffness about the landing corner is 2.9 to 31 times under the limit at which a hold keeps its error, so the ledger seats it; only an H1 with a rigid clamp is too stiff (it keeps 0.46–0.99° of a 1° error). The catch: that softness would let the sheet's weight turn a hold 10–14° if the ledger did not carry it. Hang and sway errors are swept, not measured on a robot; the humanoid model is static with gains taken as its only compliance, and the panel distributions within PS 2's limits are assumed. Monte Carlo checked against buildbot-studfind and closed forms. Stud, edge, gauge and width errors are swept, not measured; the gap, edge distance and trim come from APA pages seen in search results; stud warp means and limits come from search snippets of USDA and Wood and Fiber reports, the warp distribution shape is assumed (two are shown), and nothing is tested on hardware. Milestone 5 puts the stages in one steady-state cycle along a row: a lift stands the sheet on the ledger, the robot slides, presses and tacks it, reads the three new studs and both edges, nails with edge aim (timed by buildbot-mobilebase, 54 or 121 s) and re-drives every missed nail. On two 2x at the joint a single read a stud gives 0.9994 first-pass clean sheets at the lower warp and is the fastest choice in all 108 swept time cells: 76–216 s a sheet. On single 2x no sensing policy passes 0.59 (0.7–2.2 nails missed a sheet), three reads are fastest, and the best sheet is 17.9–65.5 s slower, all of it rework: at 30 s a re-driven nail, framing the extra joint stud may take 30–42 s a sheet and still win. Firing without waiting out a 4 N·s recoil costs up to 7.4 points of clean sheets on single 2x (a conservative model) and nothing on doubled joints, and on doubled joints a lift that hangs and tacks the sheet to 0.25° and 5 mm needs no ledger (0.978). Every stage time except the nailing is swept, not measured. Milestone 7 prices those seconds: ownership (price, life, interest and upkeep over the wall sheets of 10 to 1,000 houses a year, capped at 2,000 machine hours), supervision and the person who still carries the sheet at a loaded carpenter wage, and the extra joint stud ($3.41–5.56 retail plus a framer's time). A hand crew costs $5.21 a sheet (median; $1.93–14.46 over the taskbook's sweep of its minutes). A G1 on a drive-and-lift base costs $54, $19, $7.03, $3.48 and $2.20 at 10, 30, 100, 300 and 1,000 houses a year and beats the crew in 37% of draws at 100 and 74% at 300; a walking H1 costs about 2.5 times as much and never beats the base; a gantry in a plant ($40k–600k, unsourced) is cheaper than the base in the median draw only from about 500 houses a year. Every robot picks single 2x joints with three reads: the extra stud costs $5.42 a sheet and saves under a dollar of rework, so doubled joints pay only if a missed nail costs about $6.50 more than its re-drive. Machine prices but the humanoids', lives, upkeep and stage times are swept, not sourced. Milestone 6 rebuilt the ledger seat and slide in a second physics engine, Drake (SAP contact): a lightly pressed sheet still seats, leaving 0.0014° (1σ) against MuJoCo’s 0.00001°, and every ledger pipeline’s clean-sheet rate moves by 0.05 points at most; the press at which wall friction stops the ledger working is 97–100% of the closed form in Drake and 87–99% in MuJoCo. How far a bowed bottom edge rocks the sheet depends on the engine (0.11–0.15°, both under the bound charged), and a soft held wrist keeps up to 0.016° in Drake. Milestone 6b shows that engine dependence is an artefact of modelling the bow as three feet: a parabolic 1/16 in bow has a radius of 117 m against a centre of mass 1.22 m above it, so the sheet is a stable rocker that rolls back to level and keeps only what wall friction holds (θs = μFnr̄ / (mg(R−h0))). Both engines seat inside that band in all 48 cells (99th percentile 0.06° over 2,000 seats, against up to 0.149° charged before), the best single-2x pipeline rises from 0.560 to 0.625 clean sheets, and doubled joints move by under half a point. A kink, or 1 mm of grit on the ledger, keeps a rock of 0.05–0.15° that depends on how the sheet lands. Milestone 8 writes milestones 1–7 up as a paper draft for Automation in Construction, with a script that checks each of its 70 quoted figures against the results file it came from: three of the proposal's five hypotheses held, the gantry's crossing volume was refuted as registered, and the edge-aim hypothesis held only at a 0.5 mm stud read. Milestone 9 prices the carpenter's alternative to a doubled joint stud: pushing the bowed stud onto the line. As a Stud-grade 2x4 bending flatwise between pinned plates it takes 48 E I b / L3 — a median of 28 N and a 99th percentile of 126 N at the published warp, 376 N at the grade limit — which a stock G1 can just manage (81–88 N sideways at stud mid-height). Straightening lifts single-2x joints from 56% to 71% clean sheets at the lower warp and from 31% to 68% at the higher, but not to 95%: on perfectly straight studs the same pipeline gives 74%, so bow was costing up to 37 points and the sheet's own pose on the ledger costs the rest. Pushing each nail's point in turn, rather than once at mid-height, needs up to 1,258 N, so push first and then nail. Milestone 10 splits that 74–81% ceiling by Shapley share over six error sources: the nail gun’s 0.9 mm scatter carries 45–47% of the misses, the sheet’s pose (slide, ledger slope, panel geometry) 39–44%, the stud and edge reads the rest, and neither the tool nor the pose misses on its own (0.957 and 0.995–1.000 clean): each narrows the ±3.14 mm window the other must hit. Sliding the sheet along the ledger to centre its gap and shimming it plumb before tacking lift straight studs to 92–94% and pushed studs to 89–92%; 95% then needs a tool held to about 0.8 mm (1σ). Slide and shim accuracies are swept, not sourced. Milestone 11 measures six installed studs from the Adel et al. (2024) laser scan of a robot-built 2x4 wall (CC BY 4.0): their bows scaled to 8 ft (median 0.106 in) sit on the published mean, but 0.3–0.9 mm RMS of waviness remains after a parabola, and on the measured shapes the best single-2x pipeline gives 0.43–0.47 clean sheets against 0.58 for parabolas at the same bows; doubled joints give 1.000. Part of the waviness is common to every scanned member and is treated as scan stitching; one wall is a small sample. Milestone 12 runs milestones 9 and 10’s remedies on those measured studs: reading each stud at every nail height lifts single 2x from 0.425 to 0.530 (the waviness cost falls from 15 to 5 points), a mid push measured from the end chord adds 13 points, and per-nail reads, push, slide and shim together give 0.771 against 0.860 on the same studs’ parabolas; 95% then needs a tool held to 0.61 mm. Doubled joints give 1.000. Slide, shim and push errors are swept, not sourced. Milestone 13 prices those remedies with milestone 7’s cost model (G1 on a lift base, 4,000 draws, every missed nail re-driven), charging their seconds: a line-laser per-nail read, the push and the slide and shim (swept, not sourced). First-pass quality is cheap: three reads alone cost a median $7.10 per clean sheet at 100 houses a year (0.425 clean), the full stack $7.42 (0.771). The doubled joint stud reaches 1.000 but costs $12.17, more than the cheapest single-2x pipeline in every draw at 100, 300 and 1,000 houses a year; it pays only if a missed nail costs a median $5.51 more than its re-drive (milestone 7: $6.47 on parabolic studs). A line laser beats three point reads above about 0.23 m/s. Milestone 14 asks what a missed nail that is never found does to a shear wall, with a rigid-plastic fully anchored model (Källsner and Girhammar 2009) that tracks SDPWS’s spacing table within 6%. One joint-edge miss costs 2.0–2.2% of the sheet; with three reads on measured studs the mean sheet keeps 97.7% but the 99th percentile only 88.5%, because a misjudged stud is missed at a run of heights. Nailing the joint edges at 4 in keeps 99.98% of sheets at or above the intact 6 in sheet with every miss left in, for a median $6.98 a sheet against $7.10 with re-drives. The model loses 20% with the bottom foot unnailed where tested walls lost about half (Weiss 2017), so its losses are lower bounds. Milestone 15 rebuilds that model as a limit analysis of the whole framed sheet (a linear programme over the top plate, studs and sheet), with stud-to-plate end-nail joints at the NDS yield-limit ratio of 2.55 sheathing nails. It reproduces milestone 14 with rigid joints (0.09%), but at code-strength joints the unnailed bottom foot still costs only 20–21%: Weiss’s 40–50% needs joints at 0.46–0.56 of that ratio, or no hold-downs (64–100%), so the gap is not the framing joints at design strength. A lone sheet whose top plate can tilt loses 7% intact and 16.7% at the 99th-percentile escaped-miss sheet; a sliding top plate restores milestone 14’s figures, and 4 in joint edges carry the misses under every joint model. Design-level ratios, not tested ultimates. Milestone 16 pushes milestone 14’s sheet over with each nail a spring on the tested backbone of an 8d common nail through 7/16 in OSB into SPF (Shameli Derakshan et al. 2019: 0.97 kN peak, 0.50 kN/mm at 0.4 of it, 0.8 of the peak at 29 mm; the slip at peak swept 6–15 mm). It reduces exactly to the rigid-plastic model, tracks SDPWS’s spacing ratios within 6%, and peaks at 9.8 kN a sheet (551 plf) at 2.3% drift. With the bottom foot unnailed it still loses 20.1–20.4% at every backbone, and 20.4% for a near-brittle nail, because at the sheet’s peak the perimeter nails all slip 11–12 mm: softening does not explain Weiss’s walls, which leaves the anchorage. The escaped-miss figures stand (2.39% mean, 11.8% at the 99th percentile) and 4 in joint edges carry them. Monotonic loading only. Milestone 17 reads Weiss’s thesis in full and builds her tested wall: 8×8 ft, two OSB sheets on a single middle stud, hold-downs only on the double end studs, every nail below 12 in omitted (tested: 57% kept with 6 in edges, 34% with 3 in). The wall limit analysis matches the controls’ spacing ratio (1.93 against 1.87) and their absolute capacity to 0.89–0.92 at a tested nail strength, but at NDS-ratio stud-to-plate joints the decayed walls keep 80% and 63%: the anchorage as tested does not explain them. Post hoc, end nails at 0.47 of the NDS ratio fit both groups (58%, 30%), because the decayed wall’s least-work mechanism becomes the whole wall sliding on its 18 sill nails, which makes its capacity independent of the sheathing schedule, as Weiss found; one fitted parameter, so a tested end-nail ultimate is the check. An escaped miss costs 2.7% of a two-sheet wall on average and 10.4% at the 99th percentile. Milestone 18 adds the shear path through the hold-downs’ 5/8 in anchor rods (NDS design value 617–1,137 lb a rod): at the 0.47 fit the slide stops once each rod carries about 420 lb, and with a rigid path no end-nail strength fits (best rms 22.8 points; the decayed 3 in wall keeps 64% against 34% tested). A fit within 5 points needs each rod below about 970 lb and the end nails weaker as the rod gets stronger (a quarter of the NDS ratio at the rod’s design value, below the nail’s own design value), so a rigid-plastic model with sourced strengths does not reproduce the 3 in wall; rod slack, stud splitting and cyclic tear-out remain. An escaped miss still costs 2–3% of a wall. Milestone 19 pushes the same wall over as a displacement model (sourced nail load-slip curves, softening stud joints, an anchor rod that bears after a gap): it matches the rigid-plastic limit to 0.04%, a 1/16 in gap moves the decayed walls by 0.1 point, joints that peak early leave the 3 in wall at 71%, and no joint strength at 0.75 of the NDS ratio or more comes within 10 points of both tested groups. All 30 fits within 5 points (of 960 pushovers) have the end nails at a quarter of the NDS ratio, so a tested end-nail ultimate, or a cyclic model, is what decides the 34%. The end-nail joint’s curve is swept, not sourced. Milestone 20 put the wall through the CUREE cyclic protocol with each nail on the SAWS pinching hysteresis, fitted to cyclic tests of nails through 7/16 in OSB into Douglas fir-larch (Anderson et al. 2007) and matching OpenSees to 2×10−13: the intact peaks move 0.1%, the decayed 3 in wall keeps 70.6% against 70.5% monotonic (tested 34%), and across 96 combinations the median change is 0.2 point. SAWS has no fatigue or tear-out term, so those, and weak end nails, are what is left. Milestone 21 let every nail lose strength in proportion to the energy it has dissipated (the c = 1 form of the Rahnama–Krawinkler rule used by Ibarra, Medina and Krawinkler; the rate γ is not sourced and is swept from none to a rate that costs a lone nail 39% of its CUREE peak): the intact walls’ cyclic peaks fall to 63–97% of monotonic, but the decayed shares rise by 0.3–2.9 points at code-strength joints (3 in wall 70.6% to 73.5%), since an intact wall works its sheathing nails harder. Energy-spread damage cannot make the 34%; what is left is damage that singles out the decayed wall (tear-out along its unnailed bottom edge, the middle stud splitting) or weak end nails. Milestone 27 models the slide that milestones 10–13 credited with 0.5 mm as stick-slip on the ledger: the stock G1 hand is a 63 N/m spring along the wall (a force source in effect), so how far the sheet runs is set by the time from slip to release. Tapping from either edge leaves 0.19–0.64 mm rms at a 20 ms reaction and 2.5–10 mm at 100 ms, and the best single-2x stack goes from 0.771 to 0.79 at 20 ms and 0.32 at 100 ms (μk/μs 0.8; the OSB friction pair is swept, not measured). Milestone 28 does the same for the shim (lift the low corner until the edge is plumb, also credited with 0.5 mm): a stack of 1/16 in plastic shims leaves 0.458 mm rms and keeps the stack at 0.796, while a 1:32 composite wedge needs a 118.5 N push at μ 0.4 against the stock G1’s 65.6 N at a 0.5 m ledger, and leaves 0.13 mm at a 20 ms release because a hand weighs under 1 kg along the push (shim face frictions swept, not measured). Milestone 29 carries the tool error to where it acts: the nailer’s nose 0.3 m ahead of the grip, and the shank 44.4 mm into the stud, where a leaning nail has moved again. The stock G1’s 11-bit joint error becomes 1.31 mm along the wall (0.93 at the hand), and the best single-2x stack falls from 0.796 to 0.264 (H1 0.571); 12-bit sensors give 0.934, and an extra nail lean of 0.43° costs 2 points. Doubled joint studs stay at 1.000 (only joint quantisation is modelled; backlash and deflection would add). Milestone 30 adds gear backlash (no G1 figure is published, so it is swept to 25 arcmin): it randomises only joints that gravity and the press do not hold one way, and at the stud pose those are the G1’s two ankle rolls. 5 arcmin on every joint takes the 12-bit G1’s stack from 0.934 to 0.765; counting held joints 0.913; with the ankle rolls biased one way, no loss up to 25 arcmin. Milestone 31 carries it across 15 G1 poses (0.4–1.2 m high, ±0.15 m along the wall): calibrated at every pose, 5 arcmin costs 0.3–9.9 points (worst at the top of the reach, where knees and shoulder go loose), but both hip yaws and the waist roll flip the sign of their torque across the grid, so one tool-frame calibration leaves up to 3.4 mm along the wall; 12-bit joints then tolerate 0.44 arcmin calibrated once against 2.5 calibrated per pose (ground-reaction split least-norm, backlash and holding threshold swept). Milestone 32 makes the feet push through their soles’ contact points with friction cones: upright, the G1 balances only 26–39 N of press above 0.8 m, so it must lean 0.04–0.12 m into the wall; on the leaned poses the hip-yaw and waist flips vanish under every ground-reaction model, a controller cannot hold every leg joint one way, holding the hip rolls, hip yaws and ankle rolls cuts the worst per-pose loss to 3.7 points, and one calibration still leaves 1.1–2.6 mm (statics only; contact points from the model’s collision geoms). Milestone 33 tests the remedy: predicting each held joint’s side from the static torques and subtracting the bias leaves nothing when the compensator models the robot’s own balance controller, and with a controller that holds the light leg joints a 64-nail magazine left out of the model costs 0.017 mm (+1 kg 0.057 mm; 0.41–0.84 mm under a torque-minimising controller); a wrong ground-reaction model leaves 1.16–1.92 mm, little better than none, and a guard band on predicted torque does not help. Milestone 34 adds the joints’ elastic windup under the 25–50 N press (transmission stiffness swept, none published): with the nose free to slide, the 12-bit G1 loses 5.5 points at 104 N m/rad and needs about 1.8×104 to stay within 2; held by friction the windup only tilts the tool (0.02 mm at the nail’s tip), and at μ 0.4 the nose sticks at 10 of 15 G1 poses; an unmodelled magazine droops the servo by 32–51 mm under Unitree’s PD gains, which the encoders see. Milestone 35 treats the air hose as a force: hanging and dragged along the floor (listed hose weights, floor friction and drag swept), a 5 N pull winds the G1’s nose up 1.25 mm at 104 N m/rad and leaves the matched backlash compensator 1.0 mm, so a hose tension of 0–5 N costs 2.2 points and 0–10 N 21; the hose must come off the tool, be measured, or drag lightly. Milestone 36 measures the wrench with a wrist F/T sensor (Robotiq FT 300 listed noise 0.1 N): the G1’s residual at a 20 N drag falls from 2.34 to 0.29 mm and 0–20 N costs 1.6 points instead of 91.6, with the joints’ stiffness misjudged by 25% costing little; but even a 0.01 N error flips a held joint sitting at the (modelled, unsourced) friction threshold, leaving a floor of 0.3–0.8 mm, and the sensor’s pre-2017 version (1.2 N) is worse than none. Milestone 37 plans from the measured wrench and lets the robot settle under the true load: without a preload that costs 56.5 points over 0–20 N, because the balance controller holds its chosen leg joints exactly at the threshold (92% of the flips); holding every leg joint 0.1 N m clear of it removes them and returns 1.6 points for 1.7% more leg torque and one of 15 poses, while the 0.3–0.8 mm left comes from waist and arm joints the ground reaction cannot move. Milestone 38 adds a squeeze between the two hands along the line joining them, which has no net wrench and so moves only the arm joints: within 10 N it clears every arm flip, the G1’s 0–20 N stack loss falls from 1.64 to 0.05 points (the H1’s from 2.19 to 0.02), and what is left (up to 0.50 mm) comes from the waist joints, which only the tool’s wrench sets; the G1’s wrist pitch already exceeds its 5 N m model rating at 7 of 14 poses. Milestone 39 sets the waist’s backlash: braking it takes the G1’s worst residual at a 5 N drag from 0.485 to 0.012 mm and its 0–10 N stack loss from 5.80 to 0.04 points, a 1 arcmin waist gearbox gives 0.106 mm, and locking only the roll and pitch (as on the base G1) changes nothing because the yaw is the joint that flips. Milestone 40 brackets the nailer’s recoil from published measurements (0.09–8.7 N s: an 8d nail at chronograph speeds, and a force-plate study of framers), enough to lift the nose: the press that rises again sets none of the 56 loose joints, 36 of which change sign inside the 25–50 N window, so the spec’s 0.012 mm stands (0.203 mm only at a 20 N drag, without a compensator that plans the rise); at 12 of 35 poses, though, the leaned stance balances only above 3.7–11.8 N of press. The rise is quasi-static and the holding threshold unsourced. Milestone 41 re-leans those 12 stances 10–39 mm back so each stands at zero press and still balances at 50 N; the window’s width is (m + mtool) g × sole length / grip height, so such a stance exists only below a 1.225 m grip on the G1 (1.883 m on the H1), and the G1 at 1.2 m keeps 1.6 N to spare. The braked spec holds (0.011 mm at a 5 N drag), one H1 pose loses its controller, and the G1’s worst no-hose stack falls 1.3 points. Milestone 42 splits that loss with a two-by-two of leans and controller sides: the lean costs all 1.30 points and the four flipped leg-joint sides none, though the old sides cannot hold one re-leaned pose; compared like for like, the H1 loses 0.09–0.29 points per re-leaned pose. Milestone 43 recosts it in the spec’s own plan, which re-plans the leg preload and squeeze for each stance: the G1 then gains (worst stack 0.9160 to 0.9257 braked, 0.9081 to 0.9257 stock), so the 1.3-point loss belonged to the controller’s torques, while the H1 keeps a plan at only three of its six re-leaned poses, two because the stance allows only 0.033 and 0.095 N m of leg preload at a 50 N press. Milestone 44 gives those two poses a per-pose leg preload of 0.9 of what the stance allows (0.030 and 0.085 N m): both get a plan and their stacks do not move with the preload’s size, but with a 0.2 N sensor error the H1’s worst residual along the wall rises from 0.019 to 0.172 mm, all at (1.4 m, −0.15 m), where the right hip roll, a joint the controller holds, flips; (1.6 m, 0) is rescued at 0.003 mm. Milestone 45 gives the held joints their own margin first: the stance caps that hip roll at 0.0339 N m however much the other legs give up, so the residual stays 0.172 mm; the joint moves 0.163 N m per newton of sensor z error, so the pose meets the spec only with a z error under about 0.19 N (an ATI Mini45-class sensor, not an FT 300). Milestone 46 corrects that: the per-robot hold side pinned the right hip roll at its threshold, while the controller wants −3.8 N m; held on the other side the stance allows 2.29 N m, the pose takes the full 0.1 N m preload and leaves 0.005 mm (from 0.172) with an FT 300-class 0.2 N error, so the H1 meets the tool-point spec at all 19 poses at no stack cost; the per-robot side is also wrong at four more H1 poses. Milestone 47 gives every pose its own hold sides (the combination with the largest zero-drag margin): every pose of both robots clears the preload goal (smallest 0.886 N m), two H1 poses with no plan gain one, and the H1's worst residual at 20 N of hose drag falls from 0.032 to 0.010 mm, but the G1's rises from 0.011 to 0.037 mm (a leg joint flips under drag at three poses), so sides must be scored at the loads the robot meets. Milestone 48 scores them over 17 hose loads: the G1 returns to 0.016 / 0.011 / 0.011 mm at 0 / 5 / 20 N of drag and the H1 keeps 0.010 / 0.014 / 0.010 mm at no stack cost, but at 8 of 34 poses no side has a plan with 20 N pulling backward at the 50 N press, and the G1's worst residuals since milestone 41 cover only the 83% of swept cases that have a plan. Milestone 49 finds those missing plans are a stance limit, not a solver fault: at a 50 N press with 20 N of hose pulling back, no contact force balances the base (the robot tips back), and the drag lowers the top of the press window by about 15 N (G1 51.6 to 36.4 N, H1 58.7 to 42.8 N). Milestone 50 finds no forward lean fixes it: the best keeps the worst friction-cone slack at −0.69 to −10.12 N under 17 hose loads, because it trades backward-drag headroom for forward; the G1 at 1.2 m grips tolerates 4.0 N of hose pulling back (about 3 m of rubber hose dragging, floor friction unsourced), so the hose must be fed or carried. Milestone 51 finds those drag limits are necessary but not sufficient: every swept case past them has no plan, and inside them the G1 plans 93.0% of its cases (83.1% overall) and the H1 99.7%, in spec, but 75 of the G1’s 96 remaining failures come from its one calibration pose under sideways drag, so the calibration should be taken with the hose slack. Milestone 52 does that: calibrating under the hanging hose’s weight alone lifts the G1 to 98.1% inside the limits with no residual change, because once the compensator subtracts the measured hose load the calibration absorbs only the sensor’s bias. Milestone 53 finds the last failures are a leg-preload limit (the pose’s hold sides leave 0.004 to 0.092 N m of leg margin against 0.1), and choosing the hold sides per measured hose load gives both robots a plan at every case inside the drag limits (G1 1368 of 1368, H1 1902 of 1902) with no residual change. Milestone 54 moves off the 8-direction grid: at 48 Latin-hypercube hose loads both robots still plan every in-envelope case (9438), but 4 leave the 0.03 mm spec (worst 0.284 mm), each a joint sitting at the 0.2 N m friction threshold that the measured-load plan holds and the true load frees, in direction windows under 5° wide that the grid stepped over. Milestone 55 plans only when every joint sits further than its worst settle change under the 0.2 N sensor bound from that threshold: every planned case is then in spec (worst 0.011 mm) with no held/free flip, but coverage falls to 95.9 to 96.8%, mostly at the G1 waist and H1 torso, and the cases it drops were in spec anyway. Milestone 56 weights that margin by what each flip costs at the nose (the sum of each in-band joint’s backlash shift through the wall row of the Jacobian, held to half the spec): every planned case stays in spec (worst 0.018 mm) across three load sets, coverage returns to 100% on the G1 and 99.6 to 99.9% on the H1, and the bound is never beaten in 28 158 planned cases. Milestone 57 sweeps that share on a held-out load set: half the spec replicates (worst 0.018 mm, coverage 99.9% G1, 99.5% H1), coverage does not move between a zero budget and half the spec, the whole spec puts one H1 press at 0.0315 mm, and every flip the budget admits is a knee or ankle pitch joint that moves the nose 0.27 to 0.29 mm across the wall, the direction the bound leaves out. Milestone 58 prices each flip through both in-plane rows of the Jacobian (along and across the wall, half a 0.03 mm spec each): on a second held-out load set every planned press stays inside 0.03 mm in both directions (worst across the wall 0.022 mm, from 0.27 to 0.29 mm under the one-row bound) at unchanged coverage, 100% G1 and 99.63% H1. Milestone 59 adds the rows of the depth point 44.4 mm along the nail: on a third held-out set the two-row bound already keeps it inside 0.03 mm (worst 0.022 mm, tilt at most 0.034 mrad) and a four-row bound plans the same presses. Milestone 60 raises the leg preload, per case, for the presses the bound refuses: 0.12 to 0.18 N m from the holding threshold plans 17 of the H1's 18 (all on the left knee) in spec with no flip, lifting H1 coverage from 99.67% to 99.98% at a median 0.1% more leg effort; an elbow case and three G1 cases with no plan on any side remain. Statics only. Milestones 66 to 68 certify the sensor-bias guarantee: with the reference calibration taken under the same bias, the no-flip error is exactly linear in the bias with a sensitivity that depends only on the pose, so a table of one number per pose gates each press. On 12 held-out loads no press the gate passed left 0.03 mm (0 of 3,219) at biases of 0.3 to 1.0 N, at coverage of 64% (G1) and 90% (H1) at 0.3 N and 20% and 10% at 1.0 N; per-pose bias ratings run from 0.21 to 1.06 N (G1) and 0.28 to 1.31 N (H1). Milestone 69 adds a second calibration pose: the sensitivity re-references exactly by subtraction, so the best pair is chosen from the table, and it lifts the weakest rating from 0.21 to 0.53 N (G1) and 0.28 to 0.56 N (H1), with gate coverage at 0.4 N rising to 100% and 99.3% and still no gate-passed press out of spec. Milestone 70 lets the bias drift between calibration and press: the error is exactly J er + S d with S, the uncalibrated sensitivity, 3 to 3.5 times J, so 0.1 N of drift breaks 99 G1 and 32 H1 presses the drift-blind gate certified at 0.4 N; a gate that adds δ||S|| restores the guarantee, and the weakest pose tolerates 0.16 N (G1) and 0.19 N (H1) of drift. Milestone 71 freezes both tables and gives each press an exact drift allowance: at 0.9 times it none of 504 presses leaves spec, at 1.1 times all 503 do; the weakest pose tolerates 0.041 N (G1) and 0.091 N (H1), a re-zero every 25 and 55 minutes at a swept 0.1 N/h drift rate. Milestone 72 turns the allowance into a re-zero plan for a wall: re-zeroing as late as each press permits is provably optimal and press order changes nothing, but starting the G1’s lift bands at the bottom of its grip range halves its re-zeros (71 to 33 per 1,000 sheets at 0.1 N/h) at no extra moves, and the plan costs under 1% of the sheet cycle. Simulation only.
